entry.title: HAX Lab
entry.content:
HAX Lab is where students and junior developers learn web development by shipping real work in HAX, the open source web publishing platform built at Penn State. Interns spend a term in the College of Arts and Architecture, and each one owns one real project: a theme, the command line, the design system, the dashboard. What they build ships to everyone who uses HAX.

Find your way in

New to web development? Go from nothing to your first HAX contribution, one page at a time.

Class, clubs, the lab, faculty grants and industry, and how to join.

The Sustainable Impact and Innovation Pipeline: how a course becomes a contributor pipeline.

Everyone the lab credits, and where they landed.

Faculty who have secured funding for lab work, and how to bring the lab a problem.

What the lab built for HAX, and what it did for the students.

HAX Lab in the HAX network

The lab is one stop in a network of HAX sites. You'll use all of them in onboarding.

  • HAXTheWeb: what HAX is for and every way to get it.
  • PRAW (hax.cloud): the stories behind the lab and the people in it.
  • Build now: make a HAX site in your browser tab, nothing to install.
  • Learn: tutorials for using HAX one flow at a time.
  • Web components: every HAX element with a live demo, including ones lab students built.
  • The issue queue: work tagged for the lab.

Talk to us

Want to intern, send a class, or bring the lab a problem? Contact Product Owner Bill Rose or Project Lead Bryan Ollendyke.

entry.title: How this course works
entry.content:
Every topic is one page. Each page takes about 10 to 20 minutes of reading or watching, then about an hour of doing. Do one page per sitting. Stop when you finish the checklist, not when you run out of energy.

  • Read and watch: about 15 minutes
  • Do: about 30 minutes
  • You make: a public dev journal on GitHub Gist
  • You need: nothing yet (you'll make a GitHub account on the accounts page; come back for the journal)
  • Support level: full: every step is spelled out

Every page has the same shape

Time, what you'll make, and what you need before you start. If you don't have what's listed, go back a page.

Three resources at most. Short is on purpose: your working memory holds a few new ideas at once, so each page gives you a few.

Numbered steps you follow in another window. This is the real lesson. Reading about code teaches you about as much as reading about swimming.

Prompts you can paste into an AI assistant along with your own code or error message.

A quick question, a checklist that remembers your ticks on this computer, and a few journal prompts.

Support fades as you go

The early pages hold your hand. Later pages give you the goal and fewer steps, and the last chapter gives you a real problem with no steps at all. That's by design. It's the same path every HAX contributor has taken: watch someone do it, do it with help, do it alone, then teach the next person. HAX calls this loop SIIP, and it is how a project with one full time developer keeps shipping: students learn real skills, the best work comes back into the project, and the next group starts further ahead.

About AI

AI is your study buddy, not your ghostwriter. Some pages tell you to use it (filling in data, wiring up a fetch). One page tells you not to (the button controls), because that's where the skill you need to keep is. Claude works well in a browser tab at claude.ai. If you're on a paid plan, the Claude in Chrome extension can read the page you're on, which helps when a tutorial and your code are side by side.

Do: start your dev journal

If you don't have an account yet, make one now (see Accounts you'll need) and come back.

Go to gist.github.com. Name the file dev-journal.md, make it public, and write a first heading: ## Start here.

Why you're here, what you've built before (nothing is a fine answer), and one thing you want to make. Use ## for headings and - for list items. GitHub's Markdown guide has the rest.

You're done when

entry.title: How HAX Lab works
entry.content:
HAX Lab is one part of a loop. A course teaches web development on real HAX problems, student clubs bring their own passions, the lab gives a few students a full term on one project, faculty fund work that solves their own problems, and graduates come back as mentors. Each part feeds the next.

The loop

IST 256 at Penn State teaches modern front-end development, using HAX as the backdrop rather than the subject. Class projects often become HAX blocks. In one term, 36 students filed 24 UX findings and 18 were fixed before the term ended.

Student clubs bring what they care about. The cyber security club ran two long audits and helped fix 30 vulnerabilities. Members of the UX club applied their training to the editor.

One-term internships in Arts and Architecture. Each student owns one real project from start to release, with code review from the maintainers.

Faculty fund student work that solves their own problems, and HAX gains the capability. See Faculty and funding.

Students leave with shipped work, not just a grade. Some come back as teaching assistants and mentors for the next group. See Graduates.

A term in the lab

  • One project you own. You pick it with the team from real needs in the unified issue queue and see it through to a release.
  • Real review. Your pull requests are reviewed like anyone else's. Feedback is the point.
  • Open office hours, three times a week. They're open to anyone, and they now draw contributors who were never in the lab.
  • Public credit. With your permission, your work is posted on LinkedIn with you tagged, so employers see what you shipped.

Ways in

Onboarding takes you from nothing to a pull request. It's the same path the class follows.

Come to office hours, or comment on an issue you want to try. Clubs are welcome to bring a group.

Contact Product Owner Bill Rose or Project Lead Bryan Ollendyke. Bring a link to something you've built.

entry.title: Onboarding
entry.content:
HAX Lab onboarding is for students and junior developers. It takes you from knowing nothing about how websites are built to opening your first contribution to HAX, an open source web publishing project used across Penn State and beyond. You don't need any experience. You need a computer you can install software on, about two hours per page, and the willingness to break things on purpose.

What you'll be able to do at the end

  • Explain what happens between typing an address and seeing a page.
  • Build a card in HTML and CSS, then turn it into a reusable web component.
  • Style it with a design system instead of one-off colors.
  • Ship it: push code to GitHub and have Vercel publish it every time you push.
  • Feed it JSON data, render a list of cards, and control them with buttons you wire yourself.
  • Make a HAX site, edit it on your own computer, publish it, and pick an issue to work on.

How it's built

It's the opening weeks of Penn State's web development course, the one HAX grew out of, rebuilt so you can do it on your own schedule. It doesn't live in an LMS. You learn the web by using the web: every page sends you out to real tools, real code and real projects, then brings you back to check yourself.

This site is itself a HAX site, and its source is public at github.com/haxtheweb/hax-lab. In chapter 6 you'll fork it, change it with HAX blocks, publish your copy, and send a fix back. The course is part of the assignment.

What a request is, and the accounts and tools you'll use for the rest of the course.

Where they came from, then two cards in CodePen.

Why shared decisions beat one-off styles, with DDD and the systems HAX supports.

npm, a real web component, auditing, GitHub and Vercel.

Model data in JSON, fetch it, render it, and control it without AI.

How HAX works, hacking this course, the issue queue, and a capstone site you publish yourself.

entry.title: SIIP: how a course becomes a pipeline
entry.content:
SIIP, the Sustainable Impact and Innovation Pipeline, turns a course into a contributor pipeline for an open source project without turning the course into "the project class". Students learn the discipline. The project supplies real problems. It's how HAX kept shipping with one full-time developer, and it works at other schools and for other projects.

Why it exists

HAX went from a note card in 2015 to four full-time people at its peak, then lost developers to industry after the pandemic until one remained in 2023. Feature output still climbed sharply from 2024, because the classroom became a contributor pipeline. HAX 26 shipped the day before the talk that introduced SIIP.

How a term is shaped

A SIIP course spends its time in four parts. The onboarding on this site follows the same shape.

The SIIP term and where onboarding matches it
ShareWhat students doIn onboarding
About 40%Skill up to contributor level, with heavy scaffolding and live demos on the real codebaseChapters 1 to 5
About 20%A simple project that isn't for the community, to practice the whole workflow safelyYour card, from CodePen to Vercel
About 20%A larger project tied to the project's needs, with less scaffoldingHack this course
About 20%An unscaffolded, internship-like contributionYour first issue and the capstone

Make thinking visible

The teaching method is cognitive apprenticeship: the way a trade is learned, adapted for work you can't see someone doing.

The instructor works on the real codebase out loud, narrating decisions and not only steps.

Students do the same work with support: starter code, checklists, recorded walkthroughs.

Support drops away as skill grows, until students work from an issue alone.

Task choice, hints, feedback and rising challenge, in class and in code review.

What it has taught us

  • The biggest gains come six to twelve months after students take the class.
  • The top 5 to 10% of a class often choose to go further.
  • HAX is the backdrop, not the subject. A gap in the docs becomes a contribution, so fixing docs is part of onboarding.
  • Visible credit matters. Students' work is posted publicly, with their permission.
  • Never make contributing to one project a grade students can't opt out of. Offer another path.

The pipeline over time

entry.title: Graduates
entry.content:
Everyone the HAX Lab roster credits, newest first, each drawn as the character HAX would give them. Former lab students and contributors now work at places like Red Hat, Adobe, IBM, Ford and PennDOT.

Where they landed

In their words

  • Jimmy Kane led the team that built the first HAX dashboard in 2022. He's now an iOS engineer at Ford Motor Credit, and says the mobile-first habits from the lab still apply in Swift.
  • Winston White took the class in 2024, then built themes, much of the HAX command line and the skeleton system, and came back as a teaching assistant. He interned at Comcast and NASA before a site reliability role at IBM, and calls HAX "one of the single most impactful things for my career."

The roster

Everyone with a commit

The roster is kept in this site's own repository, haxtheweb/hax-lab. When you finish lab work, you're added to it.

entry.title: Faculty and funding
entry.content:
Faculty fund student work that solves their own problems, and HAX gains the capability for everyone. The faculty get what they need, the students get real, funded work, and the result ships in HAX. Grant sizes aren't listed here on purpose: it isn't a competition, and this work doesn't need much money.

Faculty who have secured funding for the lab

  • Bryan Ollendyke, College of Information Sciences and Technology. HAX's project lead teaches the web development course the lab grew out of, and has secured funding for lab work.
  • Dr. Blake Colaianne, Human Development and Family Studies. Director of the Learn to Flourish Hub, whose public site runs on HAX at flourish.hhd.psu.edu, and has secured funding for lab work.
  • Dr. Jennifer Frank: the International Student Portfolio. She funded portfolios international students build and take with them. HAX grew portfolio support from it, and site skeletons came straight from its needs. Because students build it for other students, she says, she never has to argue that it matters.
  • Dr. David Fusco: Canvas AI analysis. Seven or eight students, through his grant and internships, built a HAX command line tool that pulls a Canvas course through its API, reports how ready its assignments are for AI and how easily AI could be used to cheat on them, then launches a live HAX site from the result.

Bring the lab a problem

What do your students or your unit need that HAX can't do yet? Real problems make the best lab projects.

A grant or an internship pays students to build it. They learn on real work, and you get a result you can keep using.

Teaching web or software development? SIIP shows how to point a course at an open source project, and faculty resources in PRAW collect the rest.

Contact Product Owner Bill Rose or Project Lead Bryan Ollendyke.

entry.title: Outcomes
entry.content:
Lab work counts twice: once in what HAX can do for everyone, and again in what the students can do next.

For HAX

  • The DDD design system. Keith Charlton Jr turned a class exercise in cloning Penn State designs into DDD and applied it across 60+ elements. Zach Dodson then added a DDD compliance audit to the HAX command line on his own time, and it was part of the class within weeks.
  • The site dashboard, three times. Jimmy Kane's team of four built the first one in one semester in 2022; the 8-bit characters HAX still uses came from it. Ashley Santana prototyped the second, Skyler Koba and Isabella Masso built it for HAX 25, and Chloe Martin, Alyssa Foran and Winston White built the third.
  • The HAX command line and skeletons. Winston White built much of the CLI and the skeleton templating system, one semester each.
  • Security. The cyber security club ran two long audits over two years and helped fix 30 vulnerabilities.
  • Themes and portfolio work, from the Bootstrap theme in 2021 to portfolio themes in 2025. The full list is on Graduates.

For students

  • Jobs where the skills are used daily, at places including Red Hat, Adobe, IBM, Ford and PennDOT.
  • Confidence. Ashley Santana came in with almost no coding experience and described herself as drowning on day one. She left able to turn her own designs into code.
  • Mentors, not just contributors. Winston White went from student to teaching assistant to trainer, and saw his own tools change how the next students started.
  • A portfolio of shipped work with public credit, instead of a grade on an assignment nobody else sees.

entry.title: 1. How the web works
entry.content:
Before you write any code, you'll see what the web is doing when you click a link, and set up the accounts and tools every other page assumes.

Browser, network, server, database. Play with a tiny web app and break it.

GitHub, CodePen, Vercel and an AI study buddy.

Node.js, git, VS Code and the HAX command line, for Windows, macOS and Linux.

entry.title: What happens when you load a page
entry.content:
A website is a conversation. Your browser asks for something, a server somewhere answers with text, and the browser turns that text into what you see. Everything else in this course sits on top of that one idea.

  • Read and watch: about 15 minutes
  • Do: about 1 hour
  • You make: notes on a request you watched and a page you "hacked"
  • You need: Chrome, Edge or Firefox
  • Support level: full

Read and watch

  • How the web works (MDN): clients, servers, DNS, packets. Ten minutes.
  • An overview of HTTP (MDN): skim the parts about requests, responses and status codes.
  • Watch a real bug get found in a real project. Notice how much of it happens in the browser:

Play: walk the request

Walk to each part of a request. Each one tells you what it does. Touch them all.

Do: break a tiny web app

This little app is a front end, a server and a database pretending to live in one box. Everything runs in your browser, so you can't hurt anything. Press Insert and watch the numbered boxes light up in order.

Type any name, tick Main character, press Insert. Read the five status messages as they go by. Which box was lit when the SQL was built?

Open View source under the browser's table. The browser never saw the database, only that HTML. Front end versus back end, in one line.

Turn the prepared statement off. Insert Robert'); DROP TABLE Characters; -- and then Reload page. Read the SQL the server built. Why did the quote change everything?

Press Restore database, turn the prepared statement back on and insert the same text. Compare the SQL. That's the whole lesson of SQL injection: data and code must travel separately.

Do: you are a 1337 hacker (of your own screen)

Open psu.edu (or any site) in a new tab, right click the page and pick Inspect.

Click the Console tab. Paste one line at a time and press Enter:

Open the Network tab and reload. Click the first row. Find the method, the status code and the response. Compare it with the Network box in the app above.

Your changes vanish. You only changed the copy of the page in your browser. That's the front end.

Stuck? Ask your study buddy

Use AI to explain, not to do the work for you. Paste your own code or error with the prompt, read the answer, then close the chat and type the fix yourself. If you can't explain the fix out loud, you don't own it yet.

Check yourself

You're done when

Journal it

Add a heading for this page to your dev journal (the public Gist you made in Start here) and answer in Markdown:

  • In your own words, what happens between pressing Enter in the address bar and seeing a page?
  • What languages did you notice in the bug video? List every one you can.
  • What surprised you in the Network tab?

entry.title: Accounts you'll need
entry.content:
Professional web developers live in a handful of free services. Make these accounts now so nothing stops you later. Use the same email and, where you can, sign in with GitHub so everything connects.

  • Read and watch: about 10 minutes
  • Do: about 45 minutes
  • You make: five accounts, connected
  • You need: an email address you'll keep (a school address can expire when you graduate)
  • Support level: full

Read

Your GitHub profile is your portfolio. Employers read it. Pick a username you'd put on a resume, add a photo or avatar, and fill in your name.

Do

Sign up at github.com/signup. Personalize your profile. If you're a student, apply for the GitHub Student Developer Pack: it includes Copilot and other free tools.

Sign up at codepen.io using Sign up with GitHub. You'll build your first two cards here.

Sign up at vercel.com/signup with Continue with GitHub and choose the free Hobby plan. If anything about verification gets stuck, contact Vercel support now: they can take a few days to answer, and you need this account in chapter 4.

Make a free account at claude.ai and keep it open in a tab while you work. On a paid plan you can add Claude in Chrome to ask about the page you're looking at.

Open browser.hax.cloud once and look around. It runs HAX entirely in your browser, with no account. You'll build your capstone there.

Stuck? Ask your study buddy

Use AI to explain, not to do the work for you. Paste your own code or error with the prompt, read the answer, then close the chat and type the fix yourself. If you can't explain the fix out loud, you don't own it yet.

You're done when

Journal it

Add a heading for this page to your dev journal (the public Gist you made in Start here) and answer in Markdown:

  • Paste your GitHub profile link.
  • Which username did you choose and why?

entry.title: Install your tools
entry.content:
This is the page where most people get stuck, so go slowly. You'll install the same tools working developers use: a runtime for JavaScript, version control, an editor, and the HAX command line. Pick your operating system tab and follow it top to bottom.

  • Read and watch: about 15 minutes
  • Do: about 1 hour (installs take time; let them run)
  • You make: a working terminal that prints version numbers
  • You need: a computer where you have admin rights (Chromebooks and locked lab machines won't work)
  • Support level: full

Read and watch

  • Watch this terminal primer first. You'll type commands on every page from now on.
  • Node.js and HAX setup guide: the long version of this page, by operating system.
  • Common issues: read it once now. It answers most problems before you have them.

Do: install, in this order

Install Git for Windows. Keep the defaults. It gives you Git Bash, the terminal to use for this course (PowerShell behaves differently from every example you'll find).

Download the LTS installer from nodejs.org and run it. Tick the box to install the extra tools if it asks.

Install VS Code. Open Extensions (the four squares on the left) and install lit-plugin and lit-html. They color the HTML and CSS inside your JavaScript.

Install GitHub Desktop and sign in. If git is new to you, use it: it shows what changed before you commit.

Close every terminal, open Git Bash, and run:

Every line should print a version number. command not found usually means you need to close and reopen the terminal, or restart.

Open Terminal (press Command and Space, type Terminal). The first command below installs Apple's command line tools, which include git.

Download the LTS installer from nodejs.org. If you already use Homebrew, brew install node works too.

Install VS Code and drag it into Applications. Open Extensions and install lit-plugin and lit-html.

Install GitHub Desktop and sign in.

If npm install --global says EACCES, see the permissions fix in the setup guide above instead of using sudo.

Install git with your package manager.

Follow the Linux instructions on nodejs.org. Using nvm keeps global installs out of system folders.

Install VS Code plus lit-plugin and lit-html. GitHub Desktop isn't official on Linux; the git command line is fine.

Do: browser add-ons

Chrome and Edge: install JSON Formatter. Firefox has one built in. Test it: open haxtheweb.org/site.json. You should see folding, colored data, not a wall of text. You'll read a lot of JSON in chapter 5.

Keep claude.ai pinned as a tab, or add Claude in Chrome if you're on a paid plan.

Stuck? Ask your study buddy

Use AI to explain, not to do the work for you. Paste your own code or error with the prompt, read the answer, then close the chat and type the fix yourself. If you can't explain the fix out loud, you don't own it yet.

You're done when

Journal it

Add a heading for this page to your dev journal (the public Gist you made in Start here) and answer in Markdown:

  • What broke during install, and how did you fix it? (Future you will thank you.)
  • Paste the version numbers you got.

entry.title: 2. Web components
entry.content:
Web components let you invent your own HTML tags. They're built into every modern browser, so code you write today keeps working long after the framework of the year is gone. This chapter covers where they came from, then has you build the card you'll carry through the rest of the course.

A short history, the four browser features they're made of, and HTML, CSS and JS basics.

Rebuild a video card you see on YouTube.

Make a card that shares the first one's DNA.

entry.title: What are web components
entry.content:
For years every web framework invented its own idea of a "component", and every one of them only worked inside that framework. Web components are the browser's answer: a standard way to make your own tags that work anywhere HTML works, with or without a framework.

  • Read and watch: about 20 minutes
  • Do: about 1 hour
  • You make: a list of the web components hiding on sites you use
  • You need: the HTML and CSS basics below if they're new to you
  • Support level: full

Read and watch

These are the slide decks from the course. Read them in order. If one doesn't load here, open it in a new tab from the link under it.

Open the deck

Open the deck

Open the deck. The recorded lecture walks through it.

Do these first if tags and selectors are new. They go fast.

  • Learn HTML (W3Schools) and Learn CSS (W3Schools)
  • Learn CSS (web.dev) for the box model, flexbox and media queries
  • javascript.info when you need the why behind JavaScript

The four pieces

Every web component is made from the same few browser features: custom elements (your own tag names), shadow DOM (private markup and styles), templates (inert HTML you can stamp out) and slots (holes where authors put their own content). MDN's web components guide has the details.

Play: native or not?

Your character runs on its own. Jump to grab what the browser does natively, and leap over what needs a framework or a compiler before a browser can run it.

Do: find them in the wild

Open youtube.com, right click a video card and pick Inspect. Look at the tag names in the Elements panel. Any tag with a dash in its name (like ytd-rich-item-renderer) is a custom element.

Try GitHub and any news site. Write down every tag with a dash you find, and any #shadow-root you can expand.

Open haxtheweb.org. Nearly everything on the page is a web component. Pick one and guess what its attributes do.

Stuck? Ask your study buddy

Use AI to explain, not to do the work for you. Paste your own code or error with the prompt, read the answer, then close the chat and type the fix yourself. If you can't explain the fix out loud, you don't own it yet.

You're done when

Journal it

Add a heading for this page to your dev journal (the public Gist you made in Start here) and answer in Markdown:

  • List the custom elements you found and where.
  • In two sentences, why do web components outlast frameworks?
  • What still doesn't make sense? Write the question down; it's useful later.

entry.title: Project 1: a card in CodePen
entry.content:
Your first project is small on purpose: rebuild one video card from YouTube in plain HTML and CSS. A card is the perfect first thing to build. It has an image, a title, some details and a layout, and you'll find it on nearly every website.

  • Read and watch: about 15 minutes
  • Do: about 1 to 2 hours
  • You make: a responsive video card in a public CodePen
  • You need: your CodePen account
  • Support level: full, with an example to model

Read and watch

  • The box model (web.dev): margin, border, padding. You'll use all three.
  • Media queries (web.dev): how one card changes on a phone.
  • Fork this meme maker pen and change its text and font size to see how HTML, CSS and a pen fit together.

Do

Screenshot one video card on YouTube. On paper (or a sticky note), draw boxes around every piece: thumbnail, duration badge, avatar, title, channel, views, date. Label each box with what it is. This is your model.

Which parts change from card to card (title, image, views)? Those are its properties. Which never change (the layout, the rounded corners)? Write both lists in your journal. You'll need them in chapter 4.

Make a new pen. Use classes, never ids or inline styles. Start from something like this:

Keep it no wider than 400px. Space it with padding and margin in steps of 4, 8 or 16 pixels; try 8, then 12, then 16 and keep what looks right. Then add a media query so it fills the width on screens under 500px:

Use the editor's layout buttons or drag the window narrow. Check it on your phone. Does the title wrap cleanly? Does the image keep its shape?

Common mistakes to look for

  • class="thing", never class = "thing". No spaces around the equals sign.
  • No <center>, <br> for spacing, or style="" on tags. CSS does that.
  • Every alt describes the image for someone who can't see it.
  • Every tag you open, you close, in the order you opened it.

Stuck? Ask your study buddy

Use AI to explain, not to do the work for you. Paste your own code or error with the prompt, read the answer, then close the chat and type the fix yourself. If you can't explain the fix out loud, you don't own it yet.

You're done when

Journal it

Add a heading for this page to your dev journal (the public Gist you made in Start here) and answer in Markdown:

  • Link your pen and your model sketch.
  • Which CSS property took longest to figure out?
  • Which websites or videos helped? Share them.

entry.title: Project 1b: a second card
entry.content:
Now make a different card that shares the first one's DNA. Maybe it's the channel card that sits next to videos, or a playlist card. Same corners, same spacing, same type, different content and shape. Doing this by copy and paste shows you why the next chapter, design systems, exists.

  • Read and watch: about 10 minutes
  • Do: about 1 hour
  • You make: two related cards side by side in one pen
  • You need: your Project 1 pen
  • Support level: medium: fewer steps, same tools

Read

  • CSS custom properties (MDN): variables in CSS.
  • A guide to flexbox (CSS-Tricks): how to sit cards next to each other.

Do

Keep the original untouched. Fork it and work in the copy.

Move the values both cards share (radius, gap, border, font) into CSS variables at the top. Give each card a shared class plus its own:

Model it on paper first, like last time. Then build it with the shared class and only the CSS that makes it different.

Wrap both in .wrapper with display: flex. Add a third card. On a phone they should stack.

Change --card-radius to 0. Both cards change at once. That's the point.

Stuck? Ask your study buddy

Use AI to explain, not to do the work for you. Paste your own code or error with the prompt, read the answer, then close the chat and type the fix yourself. If you can't explain the fix out loud, you don't own it yet.

You're done when

Journal it

Add a heading for this page to your dev journal (the public Gist you made in Start here) and answer in Markdown:

  • Link the forked pen.
  • What did both cards share? What made them different?
  • How did copying CSS between them feel? What would happen with 40 cards?

entry.title: 3. Design systems
entry.content:
A design system is a set of decisions made once, so nobody has to make them again: colors, spacing, type, corner radius, how a button looks when you hover it. You built a tiny one with three CSS variables. HAX runs on a big one called DDD, and it can wear other systems too.

Tokens, DDD, and the same page in three systems.

entry.title: Design systems and DDD
entry.content:
Every color, gap and font size in HAX comes from a token: a named CSS variable like --ddd-spacing-4. Change what a token means and every element that uses it changes with it, the same trick as your --card-radius, at the scale of thousands of elements.

  • Read and watch: about 20 minutes
  • Do: about 1 hour
  • You make: your second card restyled with DDD tokens
  • You need: your Project 1b pen
  • Support level: medium

Read and look

  • DDD documentation: open the color, spacing and typography sections and skim. DDD stands for Design, Develop, Deliver. It began as a student independent study and now styles all of HAX.
  • Design tokens (Material Design): another big system explaining the same idea.

One page, three systems

HAX themes can swap which design system their tokens point to. These are the same quiz and checklist from this course, with nothing changed but the design system. Look at heading color and weight, spacing, and accents.

HAX also bridges Carbon, Fluent, Primer, Spectrum, USWDS, Tailwind, shadcn/ui, Bootstrap and Web Awesome. You don't need them now. You need to know the idea: content stays the same, decisions swap.

Play: the token quest

Each idea will find you and ask a question. Answer right to unlock its house.

Do

In the DDD docs, find the spacing scale, the corner radius sizes and two colors you like. Copy their token names and values into your pen's :root, for example --ddd-spacing-4: 16px;. In chapter 4 you'll get the real thing from npm; this is practice with the same names.

Replace your own spacing, radius and color values with DDD tokens. Your variables can point at tokens: --card-radius: var(--ddd-radius-md);

Turn on dark mode on your computer. Does your card still read? DDD colors are written with light-dark() so one rule covers both. Fix anything you can't read.

Open two other design systems, for example PatternFly and Carbon. Find their card. What do they decide that DDD also decides?

entry.title: 4. Real development
entry.content:
CodePen was training wheels. Now your card becomes a real web component in a real project folder on your computer, styled with DDD, checked with audit tools, saved in GitHub and published by Vercel every time you push.

Package managers, and scaffolding a component in one command.

Properties, slots, DDD and audits.

Version control and a publishing pipeline that runs on every push.

entry.title: npm and hax webcomponent
entry.content:
Nobody writes everything from scratch. Modern JavaScript projects are built from packages: small pieces of other people's code, downloaded and kept up to date by a package manager. npm is the one that comes with Node.js, and it's how you'll get Lit, DDD and every HAX element.

  • Read and watch: about 20 minutes
  • Do: about 1 hour
  • You make: a my-card project running on your computer
  • You need: Node.js, VS Code and the hax command working
  • Support level: full

Read and watch

  • About npm and package.json: what a package is and the file that lists them.
  • Intro to Lit tutorial: choose JS, not TS, at the top. Lit is the small library on top of web components that HAX uses.
  • HAX CLI playground: try the hax command in your browser if your install is still fighting you.

Do

Make one folder for everything you build, like Documents/git/your-github-name. You'll come back to it for years, so make it logical.

In your terminal:

Answer the questions if it asks. A browser window opens with your element's demo.

File, Open Folder, pick my-card. Find package.json, my-card.js and index.html. Leave node_modules alone; npm owns it.

Find the dependencies (code your element ships with) and the scripts. Run npm run to list them. start runs the dev server, build makes the files you publish, dddaudit checks your styles.

In index.html, change the title attribute on <my-card> and save. The browser updates by itself. That's the loop you'll live in.

entry.title: Port your card
entry.content:
Move your CodePen card into my-card.js. The parts that changed from card to card become properties. The description becomes a slot so it can hold real HTML. Your colors and spacing become DDD tokens. Then you let tools check your work before a human does.

  • Read and watch: about 20 minutes
  • Do: about 1 to 2 hours
  • You make: a my-card element used five different ways in index.html
  • You need: your Project 1 pen and the my-card project
  • Support level: medium

Read and watch

  • Lit cheat sheet: properties, reflect, events and slots on one page (use JS).
  • Code crit of a past class's cards: what went well and what didn't.

Do

Paste your card's HTML into render() and its CSS into static get styles(). Leave the imports, haxProperties and the translation code that the generator wrote alone; you'll use them later.

Every value from your properties list becomes a property: declare it in static get properties(), give it a default in the constructor, use it in render(). Aim for at least three: title, image and one more.

Put a <slot></slot> where the description goes. Add a fancy Boolean with reflect: true, then style it with :host([fancy]).

In index.html, make five different cards with attributes alone. No JavaScript in index.html.

Run npm run dddaudit (or hax audit) in the project folder and fix what makes sense: it points at values that should be DDD tokens. Then open your demo, right click, Inspect, and run the Lighthouse tab with Accessibility ticked. Fix every red item. Try the WAVE extension too.

Before you move on

  • All human-readable text comes from a property or a slot, never typed into render().
  • Selectors use classes. No id lookups.
  • Comment each method in plain words. You should be able to explain every line.

entry.title: GitHub and Vercel
entry.content:
Your card only exists on your computer. In this step it goes to GitHub, where your history and your portfolio live, and Vercel watches that repository and publishes a fresh build every time you push. That loop is called CI/CD: continuous integration and continuous delivery. It's how almost every professional team ships.

  • Read and watch: about 20 minutes
  • Do: about 1 hour
  • You make: a my-card repository on GitHub and a live my-card address on vercel.app
  • You need: GitHub Desktop or git, and your Vercel account
  • Support level: full, two ways

Read and watch

  • Hello World (GitHub): repositories, commits and branches in ten minutes.
  • Deploying Git repositories (Vercel): what happens when you push.
  • Watch a problem go from idea to shipped, end to end:

Do: get it on GitHub

Open GitHub Desktop. Windows: File, Add local repository. macOS: File, Add Local Repository. Pick your my-card folder. hax already made it a git repository.

The left side lists every changed file. Type a summary like Port my card into a web component and press Commit to main.

Press Publish repository. Untick Keep this code private so others can see and learn from it. Open it on github.com to check.

Change code, come back to GitHub Desktop, write a summary, Commit, then Push origin.

On github.com press New repository, name it my-card, and don't add a README (your folder already has one).

git add ., git commit -m "what changed", git push.

Do: connect Vercel

On vercel.com/new, pick your my-card repository and press Import.

Build command npm run build, output directory public. Vercel usually guesses; fix them if it doesn't. Press Deploy.

Read the build log as it runs. When it's done you get a something.vercel.app address. Open it on your phone.

Change your card, commit, push. Watch Vercel build again on its own. Your card now updates itself.

entry.title: 5. Data-driven cards
entry.content:
Real cards don't have their content typed into HTML. YouTube's cards come from data. In this chapter your cards do too: you design the data, let AI help fill it in, fetch it, render it, and then, on your own, wire the buttons that change it.

Design the shape of your data before you write it.

Load your JSON and draw a card for each item.

Add, clone, change and delete cards, with limits.

entry.title: Content modeling and JSON
entry.content:
Content modeling means deciding what your data looks like before you write any of it: which fields a card has, what type each one is, and which are required. Get this right and the code that follows is easy. Get it wrong and every card is a special case.

  • Read and watch: about 15 minutes
  • Do: about 1 hour
  • You make: a cards.json file with at least 12 cards
  • You need: your properties list from Project 1 and a JSON viewer
  • Support level: medium; AI encouraged for filling in data

Read and look

  • json.org: the whole format on one page. Note there are no comments in JSON.
  • Working with JSON (MDN).
  • Real data, from HAX: open haxtheweb.org/site.json in your browser. Every HAX site is described by one file like this. Find the items array and one item's title and slug.

Do

From your properties list, write each field with its type (string, number, boolean, array) and whether it's required. Add an id: every item needs one so code can tell them apart.

Create cards.json next to my-card.js. Write one complete card by hand so you know the model works.

Give AI your model and your one example, and ask for eleven more. Use the prompt below. Then read every card it makes: AI gets types wrong, invents fields and repeats itself.

Paste the file into a JSON validator or just open it in your browser through your dev server. A single missing comma breaks the whole file.
